title: Streaming output safety checklist and scheduler patterns
body:
Context and purpose

This is a working checklist + set of scheduler patterns to guide changes to the runtime around streaming generation. Focus is on: partial-token safety, flush/emit policies, and cancellation semantics that interact with the KV cache and kernel scheduling. The aim is to capture invariants and tradeoffs so implementation/QA/observability teams can iterate without introducing subtle correctness regressions.

Why this doc now
- Multiple regressions surfaced in evasive customer workloads where partial token emission + preemptive cancellation produced inconsistent outputs and KV cache pollution.
- We are tuning new kernel batching logic that rearranges emission timing (PR #789) — need explicit rules.
- Want to unify docs we currently have scattered across notes and PR comments into an actionable checklist for engineers and SRE.

Definitions (how I’ll use terms here)
- partial-token: any emitted token that is considered "visible" to the client before the request is fully committed or finalized. Examples: streaming tokens over SSE/chunked responses.
- atomic-chunk: smallest unit the network slices; may contain 1..N tokens.
- soft-cancel: request cancellation that allows in-flight kernel steps to finish a safe commit point (e.g., commit KV cache entries for prefix), but stops further generation.
- hard-cancel: immediate termination; may leave partial state in caches and requires rollback.
- commit-margin: stray tokens that may be buffered locally and must either be flushed or rolled back depending on policy.

Core invariants we must maintain
1) No-KV-Pollution: If a request is cancelled and later replayed, KV cache must not contain entries created by the cancelled run unless those entries correspond to definitely-committed prefix tokens.
2) Visible-Order: Whatever sequence is streamed to the client must be consistent with the final committed sequence if the request completes normally. (No reordering after commit.)
3) Idempotent-Replay: Replays should reproduce the same emitted prefix up to non-determinism allowances (sampling). If we cannot guarantee exact token equality we must provide opaque fences in the trace/response to allow downstream deduping.
4) No-Late-Flush: Flushes that happen after a hard-cancel must not cause emission of previously hidden tokens.

Checklist: Pre-merge (API + runtime changes)
- [ ] Identify all codepaths that transition "in-flight" -> "committed" states. Document callsites.
- [ ] Add a single canonical API on RequestState for commit/abort that Schedulers/kernels call (TODO: RequestState.commit(commit_point) and RequestState.abort(reason)).
- [ ] Ensure every emission path calls a compact Emit() trampoline that checks request state and applies fence tokens (see pseudocode below).
- [ ] Add unit tests that simulate: immediate cancel, delayed cancel during kernel prefetch, cancel during KV writeback, replay after cancel.
- [ ] Add integration test that runs 50 concurrent requests with random cancellations and verifies no KV pollution. (See test plan at linked_artifacts)

Flush policy patterns (tradeoffs)
- Time-first flush: flush emitted tokens after X ms (good for low-latency client perceived behavior). Risk: more partial tokens written into temporary cache structures.
- Token-count flush: flush after N tokens (good for throughput, reduces number of writes). Risk: latency spikes for short responses.
- Adaptive flush (recommended): 3-tier: immediate flush for first K tokens (reduce cold-start visible latency), buffered coalesce for tokens K+1..M with small timer, and on-critical cancel/hard-fail do rollback.
  - Suggested defaults: K=2, coalesce window=6ms, max-buffered=8 tokens. Tunable via route config.

KV cache interaction patterns
- Lease-based writeback (recommended): Writers acquire a short-lived lease on a per-request-per-prefix slab in KV. Lease ensures that aborted runs either expire leases and are cleaned or are explicitly revoked on commit. Leases must be attached to commit tokens metadata.
- Shadow-write then promote: kernel writes to a shadow namespace (request-id-prefixed keys). On commit we atomically rename/promote to canonical keys. Requires atomic rename support or a two-phase commit emulation.
- In-place write with tombstones: write directly and set tombstone on abort. Cleaner sweeps tombstones periodically. Lower complexity but increases window for pollution and requires robust garbage collection.

Cancellation semantics (recommended model)
- Two-phase cancellation: soft-cancel then hard-cancel threshold
  - soft-cancel: scheduler stops scheduling new forward passes for that request, lets current kernel run finish to nearest commit point (e.g., flush boundary), marks request as soft-cancelled; response stream gets final EOF marker and reason soft_cancel. Soft-cancel path can optionally commit prefix to KV if commit-margin satisfied.
  - hard-cancel (triggered if soft-cancel does not finish within T_hard ms or explicit user abort): terminate all kernels for request, run best-effort rollback for shadow writes or set tombstones for in-place writes; mark request aborted.
- Observability: every cancel path must emit a structured event with: request_id, cancel_type, last_emitted_token_index, committed_prefix_index, lease_id. Helps offline reconciliation.

Pseudocode: emission trampoline

function emit_tokens(request_state, tokens):
  if request_state.aborted:
    return // drop all local buffered tokens
  // ensure we don't publish tokens beyond commit policy
  fence = request_state.commit_point // highest index safe to make visible
  for t in tokens:
    idx = t.index
    if idx <= fence:
      publish_immediately(t)
    else:
      buffer_for_coalesce(t)

  // if buffer reaches threshold or timer expires, attempt flush
  try_flush_buffer(request_state)

function try_flush_buffer(request_state):
  if request_state.aborted:
    discard_buffer()
    return
  // if we are allowed to commit the buffer to KV and stream, do so atomically relative to lease
  if acquire_lease(request_state):
    write_shadow(request_state, buffer)
    if request_state.commit_decision_is_commit():
      promote_shadow_to_canonical(request_state)
      publish_buffer_to_client()
      release_lease(request_state)
    else:
      // soft-cancel or replay path
      release_lease(request_state)
      discard_or_mark(buffer)

Observability and metrics to add
- metric: streaming.partial_token_count per route (counter)
- metric: streaming.cancel.rate (soft/hard breakdown)
- histogram: time-between-first-token-and-commit (latency)
- gauge: active-shadow-writes
- log event: streaming.commit_event {request_id, committed_index, duration_ms, lease_id}
- trace span: emit_trampoline -> try_flush_buffer -> promote_shadow (span ids and tags)

Testing matrix (suggested)
- unit: emission_trampoline under aborted/soft_cancel/hard_cancel states
- e2e: 1000 randomized requests including token_count distribution skewed toward long contexts and short replies, inject network drops and kernel preemption
- performance: measure p99 latency with adaptive flush enabled vs disabled (goal: no more than +5% p99 for 95% of routes)
- correctness: KV-sweep simulation where aborted runs are replayed and assert cache equivalence with idempotent run (tolerate sampling drift)

Edge cases and open questions
- How to represent "commit_point" for stochastic decoding (sampling) where future tokens are not deterministic? Proposal: commit_point is always the last deterministic prefix (e.g., prompt + forced tokens). For sampled region we maintain metadata that allows downstream systems to perform dedupe, not exact replay.
- Memory pressure when many shadow writes are active — should we throttle by total shadow memory and fall back to immediate hard-cancel?
- Cross-request KV collisions on rename/promote — need to ensure atomicity; otherwise promote+rename can interleave. Investigate using lease compare-and-swap with sequence numbers.
- When to GC shadow namespace? Can be done by background sweeper that looks for requests older than X with no commit event. X should be conservative (default 1h) but tunable per environment.

Implementation plan and milestones
- Week 0: align on API (RequestState.commit/abort, Emit trampoline). (owners: Jordan, Asha)
- Week 1: shadow-write + lease prototype integrated with kernel prefetch path. (owner: Diego)
- Week 2: integrate adaptive flush and emission trampoline; add unit tests. (owner: Priya)
- Week 3: integration tests, randomized cancel experiments, performance runs. (owners: eng-serving-runtime + SRE)
- Week 4: roll canary with adaptive flush off by default and telemetry enabled. Gate: no KV pollution in e2e test.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally prescriptive; we want to converge on a single model (shadow-write + lease + adaptive flush) to avoid multiple incompatible in-flight implementations. If you have a compelling reason to prefer tombstone or in-place writes, please comment with workload data (expected ephemeral request ratio, memory cost).
- Pay attention to the open question around stochastic commit points — this is probably the most contentious item.

Appendix: small example timeline (soft cancel success)
- t0: request starts, kernel prefetch begins, emit trampoline buffers tokens 0..2 and immediately flushes token0,1
- t10ms: client requests cancel -> soft_cancel issued
- scheduler stops scheduling new forward passes for this request; in-flight kernel finishes and calls try_flush_buffer
- try_flush_buffer acquires lease, writes shadow for buffered tokens, promotes shadow (since commit-point >= last_emitted), publishes EOF with reason soft_cancel and commits lease
- query marked completed in audit logs; no KV pollution for later replays.

Appendix: small example timeline (hard cancel forcing rollback)
- t0: request starts, kernel buffers tokens 0..7 but has not promoted shadow
- t5ms: user triggers cancel, soft-cancel begins but kernel is hung or slow
- t5ms + T_hard: hard-cancel triggers; runtime terminates kernel, marks shadow writes tombstoned if any, emits cancel event with aborted=true; cleaner will delete tombstoned keys later.

End of doc.
